To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the liver in the chars (Salmo salar L.) and rainbow trout (Salmo gairdneri Richardson) is devoid of macro-phages, but contains specific binding sites for galactose-terminat-ed glycoproteins.
the galactose-terminal glycoprotein, asialofetinu, is specifically taken up by the hepatic parenchymal cell in char, and that this uptake is not mediated by the macrophages.
the liver is the only organ that takes up the 125I-labelled glycoprotein in the fish char.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the uptake of a glycoprotein by a fish (Salmo salar L.) liver in vivo
a galactose-specific hepatic uptake system for glycoproteins in the char (Salmo alpinius L.).
the uptake and intracellular fate of 125I-asialofetuin in fish liver cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver of the char has a specific mechanism for taking up galactose-terminating glycoproteins.
the liver of char is equipped with a galactose receptor which is able to recognize galactose-terminating glycoproteins and to internalize them.
the liver of char is equipped with a specific receptor for galactose-recognizing ligands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the galactose terminal of asialofetinu, a glycoprotein, is the recognition site for the hepatic uptake of the glycoprotein in the char.
the liver in the char (Salmo alphinus L.) is a site for specific uptake and metabolism of a galactosyl-terminated glycoproteins.
the liver in the chars (Salmo) is capable of specific recognition and uptake of galactose-terminating glycoproteins, and that this uptake is mediated by a receptor on the hepatocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the galactose receptor system for the uptake of glycoproteins by liver parenchymal cell in fish is conserved, and thus the galactose-receptor system may be an important factor in the uptake of foreign proteins by the liver in fish.
the galactose receptor is present in the liver of fish, which is in contrast to the mammalian liver, where the galactose receptors are only present in the Kupffer cells.
the liver of char is able to concentrate a galactose-containing glycoprotein from the blood.
